posts.text: In 2026 either everybody is building multi-agent systems or nobody is, and the answer depends on your definition of what counts as a "multi-agent system" (and for my money, nobody is). There's plenty of multi-agent system architectures in the literature, but they all have the same problem: nobody's using them in production, because research shows they don't work as well as a single agent does, and it seems likely that as agents get smarter that effect is going to get stronger and stronger. posts.text: Most AI governance is aimed at the wrong thing. We keep debating alignment, explainability, bias, hallucinations, monitoring and whether the model behaved properly. Fine. But none of that answers the question that actually creates institutional liability: Why was the system allowed to act? If an AI system can send the message, move the money, change the record, approve the transaction, alter the workflow or control something consequential, then the governance boundary is not the model. It is execution authority. And if your “AI governance” cannot prevent an inadmissible action before it becomes real, I would argue you do not have runtime governance at all. You have observation. That is the argument in this paper. I wrote it before much of the current industry conversation moved toward execution control. Curious to hear who disagrees — and more importantly, what mechanism you believe actually prevents the action. … more
